## Live example

```kotlin live=modifier-on-tap-gesture
TapGestureDemo()
```

## Declaration

```kotlin
fun View.onTapGesture(action: () -> Unit): View
```

## Parameters

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `action` | `() -> Unit` | Invoked when the view is tapped |

## Availability

Web · GTK · Qt

## See Also

- [Button](../components/button.md)
- [Core events](../../spec/EVENTS.md)
'''),
}

Modifiers are chainable values that describe a view's constraints and style. They
emit `PARAMETER` opcodes and never compute layout: the native element decides
how the constraints resolve.

Text("Hello")
    .font(Font.title())
    .foregroundStyle(Color.token("color.primary"))

## Core modifiers

- [Background](background.md) — paint a color behind a view.

- [Shadow](shadow.md) — draw a drop shadow behind a view.

# Pathland documentation

Pathland is a cross-platform, cross-language UI protocol. You describe **what**
the UI is with a retained, declarative view tree; the engine emits a fixed
16-byte opcode stream, and each renderer maps that stream onto its own native
elements.

> Write once, render anywhere — without a canvas and without a WebView.

## What you get

- A **binary protocol**: every instruction is exactly 16 bytes.
- A **diff-based reactive engine**: only changed nodes emit opcodes.
- **Native elements** on every target: GTK4, DOM, Qt Quick, and future hosts.
- A **Kotlin DSL** with SwiftUI-shaped builders, signals, state, routing, and
  media controllers.

## Where to go next

- [Component reference](components) — SwiftUI-style pages with live previews.
- [Getting started](getting-started.md) — build and run the Quarkus docs demo.
- [Architecture](architecture.md) — opcodes, rings, arenas, and renderers.
- [Kotlin DSL](kotlin-dsl.md) — components, modifiers, state, and routing.
- [Markdown in the docs kit](markdown.md) — what the block renderer supports.

## A first view

```kotlin
VStack(spacing = 12f) {
    Text("Hello, Pathland")
        .font(Font.largeTitle())
    Button("Read the docs") {}
        .buttonStyle(plainButtonStyle())
        .navigate("/docs/getting-started")
}
```

The same `View` tree can be mounted by a Quarkus server, a Spring Boot server,
or a desktop host. The renderer is the only platform-specific part.

# pathland-docs — implementation status

**Last updated:** November 6, 2026

The reusable Kotlin docs kit: CommonMark/GFM block parsing into Pathland views,
code blocks, tables, a `.md` resource repository, and a docs page shell. It emits
**views**, never HTML — the renderers remain the only HTML producers.

## Implemented

- **Block Markdown** (`Markdown(...)`, CommonMark + GFM tables/strikethrough):
  headings (with `ANCHOR` ids), paragraphs, bullet/ordered/nested lists, task
  list markers, fenced/indented code blocks, block quotes, thematic breaks,
  GFM tables, block images, inline links, and raw-HTML-as-literal-text.
- **Inline rendering** into `AttributedString` (bold/italic/code/strikethrough/
  links; images become alt text), with a `linkResolver` hook and `imageBase`
  prefix.
- **`CodeBlock`**: monospace, `WHITE_SPACE = PRE`, optional language label,
  padding/background/border, horizontal scroll. **No syntax highlighting** (see
  issue #188; deferred deliberately).
- **Tables**: `Grid`/`GridRow` with header styling and per-cell alignment.
  Visual only — semantic table roles are deferred with the protocol work.
- **TOC**: `MarkdownHeadings.extract` + `Slugger` (duplicate-safe ids).
- **Link resolution**: `DocsRepository.resolveLink` maps relative `.md` targets
  (including fragments/queries) to the target page's route; absolute URLs and
  fragments pass through.
- **`DocsPage.fromMarkdown`**: flat front matter (`title`, `description`,
  `section`, `order`, `route`, `draft`, `updated`, `image`), route derivation,
  and a `DocsRepository` that loads an index + classpath resources or a
  filesystem directory.
- **`DocsLayout`**: header, sidebar, content, TOC, prev/next, per-page
  `windowMetadata`, plus optional `tocOverride`/content lambdas for structured
  (non-Markdown) pages.
- **SwiftUI-style component docs**: `ComponentDoc` + `ComponentDocsPage` render
  summary, overview, live preview, declaration, examples, parameter table,
  availability badges, notes, and see-also links. `ComponentDocsIndexPage` is a
  card grid over the catalog.
- **Tests**: `MarkdownViewTest` covers headings/anchors, lists/images, code
  whitespace, GFM tables, front matter/routes, slug dedupe, and raw HTML.

## Not implemented / gaps

- Syntax highlighting (issue #188).
- Semantic table roles (deferred; tables are visual grids for now).
- Inline images inside a paragraph (rendered as alt text; block images only).
- Footnotes, GFM alerts/admonitions, and autolinks beyond CommonMark.
- A build-time docs index generator (the demo ships a hand-maintained
  `META-INF/pathland-docs.index`; `DocsRepository.fromDirectory` covers dev/tests).

---DEMO---
# pathland-docs-demo — implementation status

**Last updated:** November 6, 2026

A Quarkus marketing + documentation site authored in the Kotlin DSL. Marketing
lives at `/`; docs pages come from `.md` resources and render through
`pathland-docs`. SSR + live deltas use the standard `pathland-quarkus` extension.

## Implemented

- **Marketing page** at `/`: hero, screenshots, feature grid, a live
  signal-bound playground, component-reference CTA, footer, window metadata.
- **Docs site** at `/docs/...`: `DocsRepository` from
  `META-INF/pathland-docs.index`, sidebar/TOC/prev-next, per-page title and
  description, canonical/OG/Twitter metadata through `PathlandApp.pageMetadata`.
- **Sitemap**: `PathlandApp.sitemapRoutes()` includes the docs pages.
- **Content**: getting started, architecture, Kotlin DSL, and Markdown support
  `.md` pages; screenshots served from `/docs-assets/`.
- **Component reference** at `/docs/components` (SwiftUI-docs-style index and
  per-component pages for Text, Image, Icon, Color, Shape, stacks, Grid,
  ScrollView, lazy containers, ViewThatFits, Button, TextField, Toggle, Slider,
  Stepper, DatePicker, Picker, Menu, ColorPicker, Label, ForEach, MediaController,
  Video, and Comment), with live previews for the interactive controls.
- **Router binding**: the per-session root binds the router to
  `Platform.ACTIVE_PATH`, so deep links render the right page on the first paint.

## Not implemented / gaps

- Search (deferred).
- A build-time content index generator / live-reload content watcher.
- Docs versioning and multi-project mounts.

description: The blocks the docs kit renders, and how they map to the Kotlin DSL.

# Markdown support

The docs kit parses Markdown with commonmark-java plus GFM tables. It maps the
AST to Kotlin DSL views; it never renders HTML directly.

## Supported blocks

| Block | DSL mapping |
|---|---|
| Heading | `Text` + heading `Font` + anchor id |
| Paragraph | `Text` with inline runs |
| Bullet list | nested `VStack`/`HStack` with `•` markers |
| Ordered list | nested `VStack`/`HStack` with `1.`, `2.`, … |
| Fenced code | monospace `CodeBlock` with preserved whitespace |
| Block quote | accent bar + nested blocks |
| Thematic break | `Divider` |
| Table | `Grid`/`GridRow` with header styling |
| Image | `Image` with alt text |
| Inline link | `AttributedString` link run |
| Raw HTML | escaped literal text (never executed) |

## Inline styles

- **bold**, *italic*, `code`, ~~strikethrough~~
- [links](getting-started.md)
- nested emphasis such as **bold with *italic* inside**

## Images

![The rendered browser demo](/docs-assets/screenshot_browser.png)

Relative image paths are prefixed with `MarkdownOptions.imageBase`; absolute
paths and URLs are left unchanged.

## Code blocks

```kotlin
fun greeting(name: String): String = "Hello, $name"
```

Code blocks are monospace in v1. Syntax highlighting is tracked as
[issue #188](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/issues/188) because code is
the primary content of a protocol docs site; the `AttributedString` model and
renderers already support color runs.

# Text

Displays styled, attributed text — including inline Markdown.

## Overview

Text is the primary content primitive. Inline Markdown is parsed into style runs by default; pass `markdown = false` for literal text. Typos and code spans become `AttributedString` runs, while a plain result keeps the compact `SET_TEXT` path.

## Declaration

```kotlin
fun Text(text: String, markdown: Boolean = true): View
```

## Examples

### Inline Markdown

Bold, italic, code, strikethrough, and links are parsed into attributed runs.

```kotlin
Text("A **bold** and *italic* line with `code`.")
```

### Styled heading

A heading text style is rendered as a semantic heading.

```kotlin
Text("Getting started").font(Font.largeTitle())
```

## Parameters

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `TEXT` | `String` | The text content |
| `TEXT_STYLE` | `TextStyle` | Predefined typography; heading styles imply h1–h5 |
| `FONT_SIZE` | `Float` | Explicit point size |
| `FONT_WEIGHT` | `FontWeight` | Regular, medium, semibold, bold |
| `FONT_DESIGN` | `FontDesign` | Default, serif, rounded, monospaced |
| `TEXT_ALIGNMENT` | `TextAlignment` | Leading, center, trailing |
| `LINE_LIMIT` | `Int` | Maximum rendered lines |

## Availability

Web · GTK · Qt

state.output:
### Sequence gap detection

The network backend is reliable and ordered **within a connection**, but a
middlebox can drop a batch while the socket stays "open", and a producer's send
path can wedge — either way the consumer silently misses deltas. The batch
`sequence` makes that loss detectable:

- **Producer**: maintain one monotonic `sequence` per stream, incremented by
  exactly one for **each encoded batch**. Only guest → host delta batches
  consume a sequence number; heartbeat (`META::PING`/`PONG`) and request
  batches (`META::RESYNC`, `META::ENVIRONMENT`, events) carry `0` and never
  advance it.
- **Consumer**: the first guest → host batch establishes a baseline
  (`expected = sequence + 1`). Every later guest → host batch MUST satisfy
  `sequence == expected`; then `expected = sequence + 1`. A batch whose
  sequence does not match means one or more batches were lost.
- **Recovery**: on a gap the consumer MUST NOT apply the gapped batch (its
  deltas assume the lost state) and MUST request a full snapshot
  (`META::RESYNC`), then re-baseline on the next guest → host batch. The
  consumer also re-baselines on every (re)connect.
- **Heartbeat batches are exempt**: a `META::PONG` (host → guest) is not part of
  the guest → host stream; consumers track only guest → host batches.

The recovery is **always a full snapshot**, never retransmission: the renderer
is stateless and the application owns the retained tree, so a `META::RESYNC`
reconverges the consumer regardless of what was lost. **Acknowledgements and a
retransmit queue are deliberately not part of the protocol** — they would add a
per-session send buffer and an ack exchange to a design whose recovery is
already a stateless snapshot.

### Transport heartbeat

The **network batch backend** (a WebSocket / streamed connection) can fail
silently: a proxy or load balancer may drop the connection without a close
frame, or the peer's send path may wedge, leaving the socket "open" while
nothing is delivered. Neither side can detect this from the batch stream alone.
The heartbeat is the transport-liveness mechanism for this backend:

- **Probe**: the guest (client) sends a `META::PING` batch at a fixed cadence
  (default **every 5 s**). `A/B/C = 0`, no string section.
- **Reply**: the host (server) MUST answer each `META::PING` with a `META::PONG`
  batch as promptly as its send path allows.
- **Liveness**: a peer's *liveness* is any received batch — deltas, `PONG`, or
  anything else. A guest that receives no batch for **more than two probe
  intervals** SHOULD treat the connection as dead: close it and reconnect (the
  reconnect flow already re-syncs via `META::RESYNC`).
- **Host-side detection**: a host MAY additionally send WebSocket-protocol-level
  ping frames (browsers auto-answer) to detect a dead client and keep
  middleboxes from timing the connection out; a host whose send fails (or a
  probe that is never answered) SHOULD close the connection so the client
  reconnects instead of stalling.
- **Scope**: the heartbeat is **transport liveness only, NOT app state**. A
  `META::PING`/`META::PONG` batch MUST NOT be routed into the application — it
  never touches the retained tree, signals, or events. The **shared-memory ring
  backend MUST NOT use it**: ring peers are co-located and their liveness is the
  host process's concern, so the ring never carries, expects, or relays
  `META::PING`/`META::PONG`.

- Only a **`Fill`-sized child** fills the container's cross size.
- **The default is *hug*, not stretch.** A child with no cross-axis size is NOT
  stretched to fill the cross axis. This deliberately matches **SwiftUI**
  (children report their ideal size; a `VStack`/`HStack` aligns them) and
  **Compose** (Row/Column children wrap content cross-axis unless
  `fillMaxWidth/Height`), rather than CSS flexbox's `align-items: stretch`
  default. A renderer must therefore NOT stretch cross-axis children implicitly
  (e.g. the web renderer uses `align-items: flex-start`, not the flex default).

### Layout-greedy primitives

The cross-axis hug default has **four intrinsic exceptions** — primitives whose
native behavior is to fill space (SwiftUI/Compose precedent), so an app does not
need an explicit `FILL` frame to get their natural behavior:

| Primitive | Greedy on | Precedent |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| `DIVIDER` | cross-axis | SwiftUI `Divider()` fills the stack's available width/height; CSS `hr` is block-width |
| `SCROLLVIEW` | its **scroll axis** only (`SCROLL_AXIS`, default vertical) | SwiftUI `ScrollView` expands along its scroll axis; the cross axis hugs its content unless a `Fill` child propagates |
| `COLOR` | both axes | SwiftUI `Color` is layout-greedy and expands unless a frame constrains it |
| `SPACER` | main-axis | `Spacer()` absorbs leftover main-axis space by definition |

Rules:

- Greedy fills **only the axis the primitive is designed to fill** — never both
  for `DIVIDER`/`SPACER`/`SCROLLVIEW`; a `SCROLLVIEW` fills its scroll axis and
  **hugs on the cross axis** (a `Fill`-width content child propagates `Fill`).
- An **explicit `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` always overrides** the greedy default (`Fixed`
  = that box; `FILL` = stretch anyway; `HUG_CONTENT` = natural size).
- Every other primitive (Text, Image, stacks, buttons, controls) is a plain
  **Fixed / Fill / Hug** node governed by the size model — no implicit
  greediness.

### Non-visual nodes (layout-transparent)
|---|-------|-------------------|----------|
| C1 | `Image` `WIDTH=44, HEIGHT=44` | a row with leftover space | exactly `44×44` points (not the content's intrinsic size, not stretched) |

| C3 | `Fill`-height container | a `HUG`-height child | the child keeps its natural height; leftover stays empty / goes to a `Fill` sibling |

| C5 | Hug `Text` | a stack | natural size on both axes (not stretched cross-axis) |
| C6 | Fixed-width `VStack` | fixed `200` box, taller children | children lay out within `200`; overflow is visible unless `CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS` clips it |

native behavior is to fill space (SwiftUI/Compose precedent), so an app does not
need an explicit `FILL` frame to get their natural behavior:

| Primitive | Greedy on | Precedent |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| `DIVIDER` | cross-axis | SwiftUI `Divider()` fills the stack's available width/height; CSS `hr` is block-width |
| `SCROLLVIEW` | its **scroll axis** only (`SCROLL_AXIS`, default vertical) | SwiftUI `ScrollView` expands along its scroll axis; the cross axis hugs its content unless a `Fill` child propagates |
| `COLOR` | both axes | SwiftUI `Color` is layout-greedy and expands unless a frame constrains it |
| `SPACER` | main-axis | `Spacer()` absorbs leftover main-axis space by definition |

Rules:

- Greedy fills **only the axis the primitive is designed to fill** — never both
  for `DIVIDER`/`SPACER`/`SCROLLVIEW`; a `SCROLLVIEW` fills its scroll axis and
  **hugs on the cross axis** (a `Fill`-width content child propagates `Fill`).
- An **explicit `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` always overrides** the greedy default (`Fixed`
  = that box; `FILL` = stretch anyway; `HUG_CONTENT` = natural size).
- Every other primitive (Text, Image, stacks, buttons, controls) is a plain
  **Fixed / Fill / Hug** node governed by the size model — no implicit
  greediness.

# Pathland Layout Allocation Contract

**Wire protocol version:** 1
**Status:** Draft
**Last Updated:** October 1, 2026

---

## Purpose

This document pins down the **allocation semantics** of the size/frame
properties (`WIDTH`/`HEIGHT`, `ALIGNMENT`, `CONTENT_MODE`, and the `FILL` /
`HUG_CONTENT` sentinels) so that **the same frame produces the same logical-points
layout on every renderer** (HTML, GTK4, and any future SwiftUI/Compose target).
The protocol's sizes are **logical points** (SwiftUI points / Compose `dp` / CSS
pixels) — see the units note in [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md) — and this contract
defines what a frame *means*, not how many device pixels it is.

The wire format is unchanged by this document. It is a **contract clarification**:
renderers are aligned to it incrementally (their implementation status lives in
each project's `status.md`, not here).

- Wire format and value types: [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md)
- View catalog: [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md)
- Modifiers (the `frame` DSL surface): [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md)

> **Implementation status** is tracked per implementing project (a `status.md`
> in each protocol crate/library), **not** in this specification. This document
> defines the protocol contract only.

---

## The size model

Each axis (`WIDTH`/`HEIGHT`) of every view carries exactly one of three size
kinds:

| Kind | Wire value | Meaning | SwiftUI | Compose | CSS |
|------|-----------|---------|---------|---------|-----|
| **Fixed** | a finite positive `F32` | The view occupies **exactly that many points** on the axis. Content fits *inside* the box; a smaller parent constrains it (a `ScrollView` enables overflow). | `.frame(width: 44, height: 44)` | `Modifier.size(44.dp)` / `.width(…)` / `.height(…)` | `width: 44px; height: 44px` |
| **Fill** | `-1` (`FILL`, also `∞` normalized to it) | The view **expands to fill the available space** on the axis — it absorbs the parent's leftover space. | `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` | `Modifier.fillMaxWidth()` / `fillMaxHeight()` | flex `flex-grow` / `100%` |
| **Hug** | `-2` (`HUG_CONTENT`) or **absent** | The view takes its **natural / intrinsic** size on the axis. | ideal size (`.fixedSize()` forces it) | `Modifier.wrapContentWidth()` / `height(IntrinsicSize.Min)` | `fit-content` / auto |

Notes:

- **`HUG_CONTENT` and absent are the same size kind.** A view with no `WIDTH`/
  `HEIGHT` property behaves as `HUG_CONTENT` on that axis.
- **Fixed is a hard allocation, not a minimum or a hint.** A renderer must not
  over-allocate a Fixed view beyond its box because the parent has extra space,
  and must not under-allocate it below its box when the parent can provide it
  (a smaller parent constrains it — a parent always has the final say, as in all
  three reference frameworks).
- **Content is fitted within the box** (see [Content fitting](#content-fitting)),
  never used to grow the box.

---

## Container allocation rules

Containers (`VSTACK`/`HSTACK`/`ZSTACK`, `GRID`, `SCROLLVIEW`, and the semantic
composites) allocate their children by these rules. The **main axis** is the
container's layout direction; the **cross axis** is the other one.

### Main axis

A child's main-axis size comes from its size kind:

- **Fixed** → the child is allocated exactly its box.
- **Fill** → the child expands; **leftover main-axis space goes only to `Fill`
  children** (shared between them). A container with no `Fill` child leaves the
  leftover space empty at the end of its main axis.
- **Hug** (or absent) → the child's natural size, positioned at the start of
  the leftover space.

### Cross axis

- A **Fixed** or **Hug** child keeps its own size on the cross axis and is
  **positioned** by the container's `ALIGNMENT`.
- **`ALIGNMENT` positions but never resizes.** It selects the placement of
  Fixed/Hug children within leftover space; it does not stretch them. The value
  is a **2D position code** (the [ZStack table](./PRIMITIVES.md#zstack--zstack-0x12)):
  a stack reads a single axis (a `VStack` the horizontal component, an `HStack`
  the vertical — codes `0/1/2`), a `ZStack`/grid both axes. With no `ALIGNMENT`
  (code `0`/absent) the default cross-axis position is the **start**. Code `3`
  is `top-center`, never a stretch; stretching lives in the **child's size
  kind** (`WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` = `FILL`).
- Only a **`Fill`-sized child** fills the container's cross size.
- **The default is *hug*, not stretch.** A child with no cross-axis size is NOT
  stretched to fill the cross axis. This deliberately matches **SwiftUI**
  (children report their ideal size; a `VStack`/`HStack` aligns them) and
  **Compose** (Row/Column children wrap content cross-axis unless
  `fillMaxWidth/Height`), rather than CSS flexbox's `align-items: stretch`
  default. A renderer must therefore NOT stretch cross-axis children implicitly
  (e.g. the web renderer uses `align-items: flex-start`, not the flex default).

### Layout-greedy primitives

The cross-axis hug default has **four intrinsic exceptions** — primitives whose
native behavior is to fill space (SwiftUI/Compose precedent), so an app does not
need an explicit `FILL` frame to get their natural behavior:

| Primitive | Greedy on | Precedent |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| `DIVIDER` | cross-axis | SwiftUI `Divider()` fills the stack's available width/height; CSS `hr` is block-width |
| `SCROLLVIEW` | its **scroll axis** only (`SCROLL_AXIS`, default vertical) | SwiftUI `ScrollView` expands along its scroll axis; the cross axis hugs its content unless a `Fill` child propagates |
| `COLOR` | both axes | SwiftUI `Color` is layout-greedy and expands unless a frame constrains it |
| `SPACER` | main-axis | `Spacer()` absorbs leftover main-axis space by definition |

Rules:

- Greedy fills **only the axis the primitive is designed to fill** — never both
  for `DIVIDER`/`SPACER`/`SCROLLVIEW`; a `SCROLLVIEW` fills its scroll axis and
  **hugs on the cross axis** (a `Fill`-width content child propagates `Fill`).
- An **explicit `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` always overrides** the greedy default (`Fixed`
  = that box; `FILL` = stretch anyway; `HUG_CONTENT` = natural size).
- Every other primitive (Text, Image, stacks, buttons, controls) is a plain
  **Fixed / Fill / Hug** node governed by the size model — no implicit
  greediness.

### Non-visual nodes (layout-transparent)

Some nodes exist in the retained tree but render **no** element and take part in
**no** layout. They are **layout-transparent**:

- They are **not slots**: a stack/grid parent MUST NOT allocate space to them and
  MUST NOT contribute spacing for them (they are skipped entirely, as if absent).
- They have no box, no intrinsic size, and no content mode; `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` and
  alignment do not apply.
- Their position in the tree carries **no layout meaning** — applications place
  them for lifetime stability, not for geometry.

| Node | Role |
|------|------|
| `COMMENT` 0x7F | Opaque/debug marker |
| `MEDIA_CONTROLLER` 0x30 | Owns a media resource + transport; referenced by a `VIDEO` surface ([MEDIA.md](./MEDIA.md)) |

Audio has no node at all: an audio playback is a controller plus the
application's own views, which are ordinary layout nodes.

### A container that is itself Fixed

A container with a **Fixed** `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` is allocated exactly that box and
lays its children out *within* it. A Fixed box **constrains layout but does not
clip**: content that overflows it is drawn outside the box unless
`CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS` clips it (SwiftUI `.clipped()` parity); it scrolls instead
when the container is a `SCROLLVIEW`.

### Rationale

These rules are the bugs-fixed-and-avoided model of the reference renderers:

- A **Fixed image** in a row stays its box (never scaled to content or stretched
  by a tall row).
- A **Fixed/Hug child in a `Fill` container** keeps its size; leftover space
  goes to `Fill` children (or stays empty).
- A **composite button** (e.g. a library row) sizes to its content on the main
  axis unless the node is explicitly `Fill`.

---

## Content fitting, truncation & clipping

Content-bearing views fit their content **inside** their allocated box:

- **Media** (`IMAGE`, `VIDEO`): fitted per `CONTENT_MODE` — `Fit` (0) scales to
  contain (letterboxed), `Fill` (1) scales to cover (cropped). The box is the
  allocation, never the content's intrinsic size. A `VIDEO` surface's playback
  lives on a separate `MEDIA_CONTROLLER` node; audio has no visual at all (§
  Non-visual nodes) and is controlled by the application's own views.

### Text

- **Wrapping.** An unconstrained `TEXT` lays out on a **single line at its
  natural width**. It **wraps at word boundaries only when its width is
  constrained** — a Fixed `WIDTH`, or a `LINE_LIMIT` that needs multiple lines.
  An unbreakable word wider than the box may break by character. A wrapped
  Text's natural height is its **line count × line height** (so a Hug container
  can compute its size). A Fixed `HEIGHT` constrains the box; overflow follows
  the overflow rules ([above](#a-container-that-is-itself-fixed)).
- **`LINE_LIMIT`.** A positive `LINE_LIMIT` (N) clamps the rendered text to **at
  most N lines**; any overflow beyond the last visible line is replaced by an
  ellipsis `…` at its end (**tail** truncation). `0`/absent = unlimited. It does
  not force a single line — lines are formed by wrapping at the available width
  and by explicit line breaks.
- **`TRUNCATION_MODE`.** `Head`=0, `Middle`=1, `Tail`=2 **positions the
  ellipsis** (at the start / middle / end of the last visible line) whenever a
  `LINE_LIMIT` clamp truncates. It applies **only when such a clamp truncates**:
  on its own it has **no observable effect** (SwiftUI-aligned) — it never forces
  a single line and never truncates by itself.

### Clipping — `CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS`

`CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS` (0x1010, U8) is a **post-layout visual clip**: the node's
content and its own painted decoration (fills, backgrounds, borders) are
clipped to its **allocated bounds box** — on **both axes**. Layout is
unaffected: the node is still allocated and positioned exactly as if unclipped;
only what is painted is clipped. `0`/absent = no clipping. A `SHAPE_KIND`
(0x0006) carried alongside constrains the clip to that geometry instead of the
plain bounds box (a bare `.clipped()` is `CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS` with no shape, so the
clip is the bounds box). A `SCROLLVIEW` scrolls its content rather than
clipping it.

### Containers

Stacks, scroll, and other containers lay their children out inside; a Fixed box
constrains them (scroll for `SCROLLVIEW`, otherwise overflow is visible unless
`CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS` clips it).

### Size that fits (`SIZE_THAT_FITS` 0x17)

A fit slot is **size-taking on both axes**: it stretches to its parent's
proposal (`FILL` semantics — never hugs), because its **allocated width is the
unit of fitting**. It holds at most one (selected) child in the live form, laid
out normally inside the box; a **full-snapshot emission** (the web SSR first
document) carries every candidate and the renderer lays each one out, selecting
the visible branch by CSS container queries keyed to the slot's own width (a
no-JS correct first paint — see [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md#size-that-fits)).
The renderer measures its allocated width and derives the fit index (threshold
rule in [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md#size-that-fits)). No content-based
measurement of candidates is ever done or transmitted — the query thresholds are
app-declared, so the pick is a pure function of `(thresholds, allocated width)`.

---

## Conformance cases

These are golden vectors derived from real cross-renderer divergences. For each
case, **the same frame must yield the same logical-points size on every
renderer** (HTML + GTK4 today; SwiftUI/Compose as they land).

| # | Frame | Container context | Expected |
|---|-------|-------------------|----------|
| C1 | `Image` `WIDTH=44, HEIGHT=44` | a row with leftover space | exactly `44×44` points (not the content's intrinsic size, not stretched) |
| C2 | Fixed `220×220` child | a `280`-wide column, cross axis | exactly `220` on the cross axis, aligned (not filled to `280`) |
| C3 | `Fill`-height container | a `HUG`-height child | the child keeps its natural height; leftover stays empty / goes to a `Fill` sibling |
| C4 | Composite button, no frame | a `Fill`-height column | content height (not absorbed/stretched to the viewport) |
| C5 | Hug `Text` | a stack | natural size on both axes (not stretched cross-axis) |
| C6 | Fixed-width `VStack` | fixed `200` box, taller children | children lay out within `200`; overflow is visible unless `CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS` clips it |
| C7 | `Text` `WIDTH=120`, longer content | a column | wraps at word boundaries within `120`; natural height = line count × line height |
| C8 | `Text` long content, `LINE_LIMIT=2` | a `200`-wide column | at most 2 lines; overflow on the last visible line tail-ellipsized (`…`) |
| C9 | `Text` `LINE_LIMIT=1`, `TRUNCATION_MODE=Head` | a `200`-wide column | single line, ellipsis at the start, the tail preserved |
| C10 | `CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS=1` | a Fixed box with overflowing content | content (and the node's painted decoration) clipped to the allocated box; layout unchanged |
| C11 | `Grid` `GRID_COLUMNS=2`, `SPACING=8`, Hug cells | a definite-width parent | two **equal `1fr` columns** with an 8pt gap; Hug cells keep their natural size, positioned at Leading in their track |
| C12 | `Grid` `GRID_COLUMNS=2` with a `FILL`-width cell | a definite-width parent | the `FILL` cell **stretches to fill its column**; Hug cells keep their size; the grid does **not** propagate the `FILL` up to a Hug parent on the auto axis |
| C13 | `ScrollView` (`SCROLL_AXIS=Vertical`, no frame) | a `FILL`-sized column, content `FILL`-width | fills the available height (scroll axis); the cross (horizontal) axis hugs — it fills only because the content has a `Fill`-width child; content taller than the viewport **scrolls**, never clips or overflows the viewport |
| C14 | `ScrollView` `HEIGHT=HUG_CONTENT` | a Hug column | the viewport's height is the content's **natural height** (no vertical scroll); the cross axis hugs its content (no implicit width greed) |

Grid/scroll/lazy allocation is specified in [PRIMITIVES.md §Grid / §ScrollView](./PRIMITIVES.md#grid--grid-0x13); the lazy containers are identical to their eager base with windowed realization only.

Conformance tests (golden vectors) are wired in the renderer alignment passes
that follow this document; see each project's `status.md`.

- **Hug** (or absent) → the child's natural size, positioned at the start of
  the leftover space.

### Cross axis

- A **Fixed** or **Hug** child keeps its own size on the cross axis and is
  **positioned** by the container's `ALIGNMENT`.
- **`ALIGNMENT` positions but never resizes.** It selects the placement of
  Fixed/Hug children within leftover space; it does not stretch them. The value
  is a **2D position code** (the [ZStack table](./PRIMITIVES.md#zstack--zstack-0x12)):
  a stack reads a single axis (a `VStack` the horizontal component, an `HStack`
  the vertical — codes `0/1/2`), a `ZStack`/grid both axes. With no `ALIGNMENT`
  (code `0`/absent) the default cross-axis position is the **start**. Code `3`
  is `top-center`, never a stretch; stretching lives in the **child's size
  kind** (`WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` = `FILL`).
- Only a **`Fill`-sized child** fills the container's cross size.
- **The default is *hug*, not stretch.** A child with no cross-axis size is NOT
  stretched to fill the cross axis. This deliberately matches **SwiftUI**
  (children report their ideal size; a `VStack`/`HStack` aligns them) and
  **Compose** (Row/Column children wrap content cross-axis unless
  `fillMaxWidth/Height`), rather than CSS flexbox's `align-items: stretch`
  default. A renderer must therefore NOT stretch cross-axis children implicitly
  (e.g. the web renderer uses `align-items: flex-start`, not the flex default).

### Layout-greedy primitives

The cross-axis hug default has **four intrinsic exceptions** — primitives whose
native behavior is to fill space (SwiftUI/Compose precedent), so an app does not
need an explicit `FILL` frame to get their natural behavior:

| Primitive | Greedy on | Precedent |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| `DIVIDER` | cross-axis | SwiftUI `Divider()` fills the stack's available width/height; CSS `hr` is block-width |
| `SCROLLVIEW` | its **scroll axis** only (`SCROLL_AXIS`, default vertical) | SwiftUI `ScrollView` expands along its scroll axis; the cross axis hugs its content unless a `Fill` child propagates |
| `COLOR` | both axes | SwiftUI `Color` is layout-greedy and expands unless a frame constrains it |
| `SPACER` | main-axis | `Spacer()` absorbs leftover main-axis space by definition |

Rules:

- Greedy fills **only the axis the primitive is designed to fill** — never both
  for `DIVIDER`/`SPACER`/`SCROLLVIEW`; a `SCROLLVIEW` fills its scroll axis and
  **hugs on the cross axis** (a `Fill`-width content child propagates `Fill`).
- An **explicit `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` always overrides** the greedy default (`Fixed`
  = that box; `FILL` = stretch anyway; `HUG_CONTENT` = natural size).
- Every other primitive (Text, Image, stacks, buttons, controls) is a plain
  **Fixed / Fill / Hug** node governed by the size model — no implicit
  greediness.

### Non-visual nodes (layout-transparent)

Some nodes exist in the retained tree but render **no** element and take part in
**no** layout. They are **layout-transparent**:

- They are **not slots**: a stack/grid parent MUST NOT allocate space to them and
  MUST NOT contribute spacing for them (they are skipped entirely, as if absent).
- They have no box, no intrinsic size, and no content mode; `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` and
  alignment do not apply.
- Their position in the tree carries **no layout meaning** — applications place
  them for lifetime stability, not for geometry.

| Node | Role |
|------|------|
| `COMMENT` 0x7F | Opaque/debug marker |
| `MEDIA_CONTROLLER` 0x30 | Owns a media resource + transport; referenced by a `VIDEO` surface ([MEDIA.md](./MEDIA.md)) |

Audio has no node at all: an audio playback is a controller plus the
application's own views, which are ordinary layout nodes.

### A container that is itself Fixed

A container with a **Fixed** `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` is allocated exactly that box and
lays its children out *within* it. A Fixed box **constrains layout but does not
clip**: content that overflows it is drawn outside the box unless
`CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS` clips it (SwiftUI `.clipped()` parity); it scrolls instead
when the container is a `SCROLLVIEW`.

### Rationale

These rules are the bugs-fixed-and-avoided model of the reference renderers:

- A **Fixed image** in a row stays its box (never scaled to content or stretched
  by a tall row).
- A **Fixed/Hug child in a `Fill` container** keeps its size; leftover space
  goes to `Fill` children (or stays empty).
- A **composite button** (e.g. a library row) sizes to its content on the main
  axis unless the node is explicitly `Fill`.

---

## Content fitting, truncation & clipping

Content-bearing views fit their content **inside** their allocated box:

- **Media** (`IMAGE`, `VIDEO`): fitted per `CONTENT_MODE` — `Fit` (0) scales to
  contain (letterboxed), `Fill` (1) scales to cover (cropped). The box is the
  allocation, never the content's intrinsic size. A `VIDEO` surface's playback
  lives on a separate `MEDIA_CONTROLLER` node; audio has no visual at all (§
  Non-visual nodes) and is controlled by the application's own views.

### Text

- **Wrapping.** An unconstrained `TEXT` lays out on a **single line at its
  natural width**. It **wraps at word boundaries only when its width is
  constrained** — a Fixed `WIDTH`, or a `LINE_LIMIT` that needs multiple lines.
  An unbreakable word wider than the box may break by character. A wrapped
  Text's natural height is its **line count × line height** (so a Hug container
  can compute its size). A Fixed `HEIGHT` constrains the box; overflow follows
  the overflow rules ([above](#a-container-that-is-itself-fixed)).
- **`LINE_LIMIT`.** A positive `LINE_LIMIT` (N) clamps the rendered text to **at
  most N lines**; any overflow beyond the last visible line is replaced by an
  ellipsis `…` at its end (**tail** truncation). `0`/absent = unlimited. It does
  not force a single line — lines are formed by wrapping at the available width
  and by explicit line breaks.
- **`TRUNCATION_MODE`.** `Head`=0, `Middle`=1, `Tail`=2 **positions the
  ellipsis** (at the start / middle / end of the last visible line) whenever a
  `LINE_LIMIT` clamp truncates. It applies **only when such a clamp truncates**:
  on its own it has **no observable effect** (SwiftUI-aligned) — it never forces
  a single line and never truncates by itself.

### Clipping — `CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS`

`CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS` (0x1010, U8) is a **post-layout visual clip**: the node's
content and its own painted decoration (fills, backgrounds, borders) are
clipped to its **allocated bounds box** — on **both axes**. Layout is
unaffected: the node is still allocated and positioned exactly as if unclipped;
only what is painted is clipped. `0`/absent = no clipping. A `SHAPE_KIND`
(0x0006) carried alongside constrains the clip to that geometry instead of the
plain bounds box (a bare `.clipped()` is `CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS` with no shape, so the
clip is the bounds box). A `SCROLLVIEW` scrolls its content rather than
clipping it.

### Containers

Stacks, scroll, and other containers lay their children out inside; a Fixed box
constrains them (scroll for `SCROLLVIEW`, otherwise overflow is visible unless
`CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS` clips it).

### Size that fits (`SIZE_THAT_FITS` 0x17)

A fit slot is **size-taking on both axes**: it stretches to its parent's
proposal (`FILL` semantics — never hugs), because its **allocated width is the
unit of fitting**. It holds at most one (selected) child in the live form, laid
out normally inside the box; a **full-snapshot emission** (the web SSR first
document) carries every candidate and the renderer lays each one out, selecting
the visible branch by CSS container queries keyed to the slot's own width (a
no-JS correct first paint — see [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md#size-that-fits)).
The renderer measures its allocated width and derives the fit index (threshold
rule in [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md#size-that-fits)). No content-based
measurement of candidates is ever done or transmitted — the query thresholds are
app-declared, so the pick is a pure function of `(thresholds, allocated width)`.

---

## Conformance cases

These are golden vectors derived from real cross-renderer divergences. For each
case, **the same frame must yield the same logical-points size on every
renderer** (HTML + GTK4 today; SwiftUI/Compose as they land).

| # | Frame | Container context | Expected |
|---|-------|-------------------|----------|
| C1 | `Image` `WIDTH=44, HEIGHT=44` | a row with leftover space | exactly `44×44` points (not the content's intrinsic size, not stretched) |
| C2 | Fixed `220×220` child | a `280`-wide column, cross axis | exactly `220` on the cross axis, aligned (not filled to `280`) |
| C3 | `Fill`-height container | a `HUG`-height child | the child keeps its natural height; leftover stays empty / goes to a `Fill` sibling |
| C4 | Composite button, no frame | a `Fill`-height column | content height (not absorbed/stretched to the viewport) |
| C5 | Hug `Text` | a stack | natural size on both axes (not stretched cross-axis) |
| C6 | Fixed-width `VStack` | fixed `200` box, taller children | children lay out within `200`; overflow is visible unless `CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS` clips it |
| C7 | `Text` `WIDTH=120`, longer content | a column | wraps at word boundaries within `120`; natural height = line count × line height |
| C8 | `Text` long content, `LINE_LIMIT=2` | a `200`-wide column | at most 2 lines; overflow on the last visible line tail-ellipsized (`…`) |
| C9 | `Text` `LINE_LIMIT=1`, `TRUNCATION_MODE=Head` | a `200`-wide column | single line, ellipsis at the start, the tail preserved |
| C10 | `CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS=1` | a Fixed box with overflowing content | content (and the node's painted decoration) clipped to the allocated box; layout unchanged |
| C11 | `Grid` `GRID_COLUMNS=2`, `SPACING=8`, Hug cells | a definite-width parent | two **equal `1fr` columns** with an 8pt gap; Hug cells keep their natural size, positioned at Leading in their track |
| C12 | `Grid` `GRID_COLUMNS=2` with a `FILL`-width cell | a definite-width parent | the `FILL` cell **stretches to fill its column**; Hug cells keep their size; the grid does **not** propagate the `FILL` up to a Hug parent on the auto axis |
| C13 | `ScrollView` (`SCROLL_AXIS=Vertical`, no frame) | a `FILL`-sized column, content `FILL`-width | fills the available height (scroll axis); the cross (horizontal) axis hugs — it fills only because the content has a `Fill`-width child; content taller than the viewport **scrolls**, never clips or overflows the viewport |
| C14 | `ScrollView` `HEIGHT=HUG_CONTENT` | a Hug column | the viewport's height is the content's **natural height** (no vertical scroll); the cross axis hugs its content (no implicit width greed) |

Grid/scroll/lazy allocation is specified in [PRIMITIVES.md §Grid / §ScrollView](./PRIMITIVES.md#grid--grid-0x13); the lazy containers are identical to their eager base with windowed realization only.

Conformance tests (golden vectors) are wired in the renderer alignment passes
that follow this document; see each project's `status.md`.

74-## Architectural Rules
75-
76-### 1. Core Structural Classification
77-
78-Each node belongs to exactly one of the three categories above. The category
79-determines renderer responsibilities:
80-
81-- **Primitive Drawing Nodes** hold no interaction state. The server sends the
82-  full visual description; the renderer measures and paints. If a primitive has
83-  no native equivalent (e.g. `Path`), the renderer may paint it directly — this
84-  is the one case where canvas-style painting is permitted.
85-- **Semantic Control Nodes** carry intent + two-way bindings (`BINDING_ID`),
86-  accessibility traits, and local interaction physics. Their *visual chrome* is
87-  delegated per the Dual-Mode rules below; their *interaction semantics* are
88-  always renderer-owned and reported as raw events.
89-
90-### 2. Dual-Mode Rendering Pipeline & Platform Delegation
91-
92-Every semantic control node renders in **one of two modes**, decided by whether
93-the node has a child layout tree:
94-
95-#### Native Token Mode (Leaf Control)
96-
97-When a semantic control node has **no child layout tree** (`childrenIds` is
98-empty), the client platform **MUST delegate rendering entirely to its native OS
99-control** — `Button`, `TextField`/`SecureField`, `Toggle`, `Slider`, `Stepper`,
100-`DatePicker`, `ColorPicker`, `Picker`, and `Menu` each map to the platform's
101-native control (the concrete widget per renderer lives in that renderer's
102-`status.md`).
103-
104-**System style modifiers act as visual style tokens** — they force the platform
105-to switch native control variants **without emitting child nodes over the
106-wire**. Example: `TOGGLE_STYLE = CHECKBOX` renders `Toggle` (0x24) as a native
107-checkbox; `TOGGLE_STYLE = SWITCH` (default) as a native switch; `TOGGLE_STYLE =
108-BUTTON` as a toggle button.
109-
110-#### Composite Override Mode (Container Control)
111-
112-When a semantic control **contains child nodes** (or a custom style body is
113-defined on the server), the client platform **MUST**:
114-
115-1. **Suppress** its default native control visuals (the OS control chrome).

### ScrollView — `SCROLLVIEW` 0x14

A scrollable content container. **Layout-greedy on its scroll axis** — it fills
the available space on that axis so the content can scroll; on the **cross axis**
it **hugs its content** by default (it shrinks to fit the content, SwiftUI
`ScrollView` semantics). An explicit `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` overrides either behavior
(LAYOUT.md §layout-greedy primitives).

**Content.** The **first child** is the content; a scroll view carries a single
content subtree (typically a stack), matching SwiftUI/Compose's single-content
contract. The content is measured with an **unbounded proposal on the scroll
axis** — it may grow beyond the viewport (that is what scrolls) — and a
**bounded proposal on the cross axis** (the viewport's cross size). **Fill
propagation applies on the cross axis**: a `Fill`-width child of the content

fills the viewport on that axis — so a full-width scroll row is authored as a
`Fill`-width child, never by stretching the content or the viewport. Content
with no `Fill` child keeps its natural cross size, and the viewport hugs/shrinks
to fit it. The **viewport** is the scroll view's allocated box; a Hug
`WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` — or a Hug parent proposal on an axis — sizes the viewport to
the content's natural size on that axis (the viewport fits the content, so that
axis does not scroll).

viewport clips by virtue of scrolling; `CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS` on the scroll view has

parts.text:
Great. Qt already correct on scroll axis and HUG. GTK not. Need align HTML/TS/GTK with spec and Qt. Also need determine maxWidth behavior. Qt `effectiveFill` treats fixed/hug dimensions as bounding but doesn't mention MAX_WIDTH. GTK likely ignores bounds. HTML/TS ignore bounds in layout. So finite maxWidth with auto width + fill descendant: current behavior sets width:100% and max-width, and align-self stretch. The user expects center. The spec currently does not define maxWidth interaction. We need decide correct semantics and update spec first.

We need identify what "spec correct" means. Likely:
- Clarify `MIN/IDEAL/MAX` frame bounds semantics: bounds are constraints on the node's allocated size, not a size kind. They apply after the size kind (Fixed/Fill/Hug) and before positioning. A finite max width caps FILL and limits Hug growth; a finite min raises Hug/Fixed? Need precise.
- Define that bounds do not change the node's size kind or fill propagation. Hmm. If maxWidth caps fill, then a Hug node with maxWidth? In SwiftUI, `.frame(maxWidth: 620)` creates a flexible frame that can expand up to 620. It is not simply a cap on the inner view; it's a frame that fills available up to max. The current DSL `frame { maxWidth(620f) }` likely intends SwiftUI semantics. But the current renderer uses only CSS max-width on the node, not a wrapper; if the node has no width, its width is auto, so max-width does nothing (auto width sizes to content, then max caps). If node has fill due to content, width 100% then max cap. So semantics:
  - For a Hug node with maxWidth, it should be at most maxWidth but otherwise Hug. If its content is greedy/fill, it can expand up to maxWidth. This is "bounded hug/fill." Parent alignment should center if space > max.
  - For a Fill node with maxWidth, it should fill up to maxWidth and be positioned by parent alignment in leftover space. 
  - For a Fixed node with maxWidth less than fixed? SwiftUI frame order matters: `.frame(width:...)` vs `.frame(maxWidth:...)` are separate frames; in Pathland both properties are on the same node, so we need precedence. The protocol doesn't encode ordering. Existing code writes WIDTH then MAX_WIDTH; CSS clamps. So bounds capproperties. Fixed > max => max wins (clamped). That's current behavior. Spec should state bounds clamp the resolved size.
- The core issue: `fills_axis` should consider max bounds when deciding propagation/placement:
  - A node with a finite `MAX_WIDTH`/`MAX_HEIGHT` should not be considered unbounded FILL beyond that max. But it may still be Fill up to the max. For the parent cross-axis:

HTML status says frame bounds only emitted, not used in layout. Need update status after fix.

Need inspect `pathland-render-html/status.md` scroll section says greedy both axes; will update. Good.

Now spec correction specifics. We need formulate exact text. Let's design a coherent bounds model that is implementable across CSS, GTK, Qt.

Maybe instead of a complex enum, define a clear simple model:
- **Bounds are clamps on the resolved size.**
- **A finite max bound suppresses fill propagation** on that axis and **prevents cross-axis stretch**; the node is positioned by the parent's ALIGNMENT. This means:
  - Hug + max: natural size up to max; centered by parent.
  - Fill + max: fills available up to max; then centered by parent (CSS width 100% max-width + no align-self stretch).
  - Greedy primitive + max: greed up to max; centered.
  - Ancestors do not inherit an *unbounded* fill from a max-bounded descendant; they size to content (which is capped), so they also center.
- This may be called **bounded fill**. No need for a 4th size kind; it's a clamped Fill/Hug.
- **Implementation rule:** For layout propagation and cross-axis stretch, treat a node with a finite max on an axis as "not unbounded fill"; it still fills/clamps its own CSS size if it is FILL/greedy, but does not force ancestors to 100% and does not add `align-self:stretch`. The node's own max-width caps it and parent alignment positions it.
- **Main-axis:** bounded fill still participates as fill up to its max; leftover after max remains at the end. This is consistent.
- **Min bound:** raises the resolved size; can make a Hug node larger than content. It does not create fill. CSS min-width handles. For fill propagation, min does not make it fill; no. It may make ancestor larger? A Hug ancestor with a min-width child will size to min; okay via content.
- **Ideal:** define as a preferred natural size when the axis is Hug; if content has an intrinsic size, ideal is ignored? Hmm. In CSS, setting width from ideal overrides content, effectively Fixed. We need be careful. Maybe define `IDEAL_*` as "the node's preferred size when the axis is Hug and the content has no intrinsic size; otherwise advisory." Implementation currently maps to CSS width, which acts as Fixed. That conflicts. Could exclude IDEAL from this fix? But spec correctness. Let's examine if IDEAL is used anywhere in code/demos. Search.

# Plan: spec-first ScrollView / frame-bounds layout fix

## Spec audit — what is already correct

`spec/LAYOUT.md` already states the right contract:

- `SCROLLVIEW` is greedy **only on its scroll axis**; the cross axis hugs and only fills via a `Fill` content child (`LAYOUT.md:105`, C13/C14).
- `ALIGNMENT` positions, never stretches; only FILL children stretch.
- `PRIMITIVES.md §ScrollView` matches that.

The renderers are the inconsistent part:

- Rust HTML: `fills_axis` treats `SCROLLVIEW` as greedy on both axes (`lib/rust/.../lib.rs:697`), emits unconditional `flex:1 1 auto;align-self:stretch` (`:2095`), and ignores `SCROLL_AXIS`.
- Java HTML port: same (`HtmlRenderer.java:743`, `RenderNode.java:519`).
- TS DOM: same (`apply.ts:166-170`, `elements.ts:91-98`).
- GTK: documents `SCROLL_AXIS` as a gap (`render-gtk/status.md`).
- Qt: already implements axis-aware ScrollView greed (`qt_layer.cpp:1044`), so it is the reference for that part.

## Spec corrections needed first

### 1. Add a “Frame bounds” section to `spec/LAYOUT.md`

Bounds (`MIN_*`, `IDEAL_*`, `MAX_*`) currently have no layout contract at all; the docs only say they are emitted. Define:

- Bounds are constraints layered on top of the size kind, not new size kinds.
- Resolution order per axis: base size kind/intrinsic size → apply bounds → position.
- `MIN_*` raises the resolved size; `MAX_*` caps it; if `MIN > MAX`, `MIN` wins.
- A finite `MAX_*` makes the axis **bounded**:
  - A `Fill` or greedy node still fills/grows up to the cap.
  - A `Hug` node remains Hug, capped by the max.
  - A bounded node does **not** propagate an unbounded fill to ancestors.
  - A bounded node is **not** given cross-axis stretch; once capped, it is positioned by the parent’s `ALIGNMENT`.
- `IDEAL_*`: recommended spec choice is an advisory Hug preference; v1 renderers may ignore it rather than treating it as Fixed. This fixes the current CSS mapping where `IDEAL_WIDTH` overwrites `WIDTH`.
- `MAX_* = ∞` means “no constraint” and is omitted; `WIDTH/HEIGHT = ∞` means `FILL`.

### 2. Resolve the infinity contradiction

`MODIFIERS.md:67` says `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` ⇔ `WIDTH=FILL`; `DSL.md:850` says infinite `maxWidth` in the bounds builder means “no limit.” Clarify:

- Canonical SwiftUI `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` is represented as `WIDTH=FILL`.
- The explicit `MAX_WIDTH`/`MAX_HEIGHT` properties are finite bounds only; an infinite value is omitted.
- Update the DSL sentence to match.

### 3. Tighten ScrollView wording

Add to `PRIMITIVES.md §ScrollView` and `LAYOUT.md`:

- A finite `MAX_*` on the scroll axis caps the viewport’s greedy size.
- A finite `MAX_*` on the cross axis caps content fill propagation; the viewport is positioned by the parent’s `ALIGNMENT`.
- Explicit `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` still overrides greed.

### 4. Add conformance cases C15–C20

- Horizontal `SCROLLVIEW`: width greedy, height hugs.
- Vertical `SCROLLVIEW` with `FILL`-width content: height greedy, width fills from content.
- `Hug` child with finite `MAX_WIDTH` in a centered `VStack`: capped and centered; no `width:100%`, no `align-self:stretch`.
- `FILL` child with finite `MAX_WIDTH`: fills up to cap, then centered by parent alignment.
- `MIN > MAX`: min wins.
- Bounded ScrollView cross-axis fill: capped, not propagated as unbounded.

No wire-format or `protocol.tsv` changes.

## Implementation plan

### Phase A — canonical Rust HTML renderer

Files: `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/src/lib.rs`, tests.

1. Make `SCROLLVIEW` greed axis-aware via `SCROLL_AXIS` (default vertical).
2. Add finite-max detection to the fill-demand decision:
   - `fills_axis` returns false for a bounded axis for propagation/cross-stretch purposes.
   - A node’s own explicit `WIDTH/HEIGHT=FILL` still emits `width/height:100%`; the finite max caps it.
3. Stop emitting unconditional `flex:1 1 auto;align-self:stretch` for ScrollView. Derive scroll fill from:
   - `SCROLL_AXIS`,
   - the parent stack’s main axis,
   - the scroll node’s own size hints/bounds.
4. Emit `data-pathland-scroll-axis="vertical|horizontal"` on ScrollView elements for DOM hydration.
5. Emit `align-self:stretch` only for **unbounded** fill. Omit it for bounded/non-fill so parent `align-items` (center/start/end) positions the capped box.
6. Keep `fill_propagation` from adding `width/height:100%` when the axis is bounded.
7. Add tests for `SCROLL_AXIS`, bounded max placement, and C13–C20.

### Phase B — Java HTML port

Files: `RenderNode.java`, `HtmlRenderer.java`, tests.

Mirror Phase A exactly:

### Phase C — TypeScript DOM renderer

Files: `constants.ts`, `classes.ts`, `elements.ts`, `apply.ts`, transport/tests.

1. Add `PROP_SCROLL_AXIS` handling; read `data-pathland-scroll-axis` for hydrated SSR nodes and default to vertical.
2. Make `fillsAxis` axis-aware for ScrollView.
3. Treat finite `maxWidth`/`maxHeight` as bounded:
   - do not classify as unbounded fill,
   - clear `align-self` so the parent’s `align-items` centers/positions it,
   - preserve explicit `width:100%` from FILL (max-width clamps it).
4. Remove the unconditional scroll `flex/align-self`; derive scroll fill from axis + parent orientation in `applyLayout`.
5. Ensure the layout pass clears stale derived `width/height/align-self` when a node stops being fill. Track layout-owned properties (or recompute them explicitly) so removing Spacers cannot leave a stale `width:100%`.
6. Skip `applyBatch` for transport-only `META::PONG` batches so heartbeats stop re-running `applyLayout` (spec: PING/PONG must not reach the application).

- **Qt**: already axis-aware; update `effectiveFill`/`applyChildAxes` so bounded max children are positioned by parent alignment instead of stretched. Add tests.
- **GTK**: implement `SCROLL_AXIS` (known gap). Finite `MAX_*` needs a wrapper or custom allocation because GTK has no max-size API; otherwise leave as a documented gap.
- Update `render-gtk/status.md` and `render-qt/status.md` accordingly.

Recommended scope for this change: **spec + Rust HTML + Java HTML + TS DOM + fixtures** (the reported bug and the cross-language HTML contract). Do GTK/Qt as a follow-up unless you want native parity in the same change.

### Phase F — docs site verification

No `DocsSite.kt` layout workaround should be necessary. After the fix, `/` should produce:

- HStack `#40`: no `width:100%`, no `height:100%`, no `align-self:stretch`;

parts.text:
We have enough. Need also maybe fetch SwiftUI docs exact for ideal behavior. Search excerpt gives the algorithm:
- "The size proposed to this view is the size proposed to the frame, limited by any constraints specified, and with any ideal dimensions specified replacing any corresponding unspecified dimensions in the proposal."
- If no min/max, frame adopts child behavior. If both min and max specified, adopts proposed size clamped. Otherwise:
  - if min specified and parent proposal < view size, proposed clamped to min.
  - if max specified and parent proposal > view size, proposed clamped to max.
  - otherwise view size.
This is subtle. For only maxWidth finite: final size = clamp? According to onmyway133 scenario 3: `clamp(contentWidth, parentWidth, maxWidth)` = min(max(contentWidth, parentWidth?), max?) Wait `clamp(content, parent, max)` with Swift's clamp order? They likely mean min(max(content, parent?), max). Actually SwiftUI docs say:
- only max: size = min(max(proposal, view size), max)? Let's parse:
  - "If a maximum constraint is specified and the size proposed for the frame by the parent is greater than the size of this view, the proposed size, clamped to that maximum." So if parent proposal > view size, frame size = min(parent proposal, max). If parent proposal <= view size, "Otherwise, the size of this view" (view size). So only max: final = view size if parent proposal <= view size; else min(parent proposal, max). This means it can expand up to max if parent proposes more, even if content smaller! Yes, because if parent proposal > view size, frame takes the proposal clamped to max. Example: Text width 50, parent proposes 1000, maxWidth 620 -> frame 620. So SwiftUI maxWidth finite DOES fill up to max when parent proposes more. The Stack Overflow confirms. The SwiftUI Lab's "It sets final size to max whenever content size bigger than max, otherwise content size" contradicts? Hmm, maybe their test parent proposes 300 and content 40, max 40? Let's trust Apple docs: only max, parent proposal greater than view size -> proposed size clamped to max. So fills to max if parent proposes larger. Thus SwiftUI maxWidth is a flexible fill-up-to-max, not a cap/hug when parent is larger. That's important.
- If parent proposal is unconstrained (nil), maybe ideal. If proposal unspecified, only max? Then frame size = view size? Hmm.
- So if we want to match SwiftUI, `MAX_WIDTH` finite on a Hug node should fill to max when parent offers more, and be positioned by alignment. The docs page first HStack `.frame(maxWidth:1240)` would become 1240 if parent offers 1240, not hug 1180. The second HStack max 1240 would become 1240, not hug 700, and not centered at 700. So the user's desired "center both HStacks" would not be achieved by simply maxWidth; they'd need a parent `HStack`/`VStack` with alignment and a fixed/hug inner width, or Spacers. This is important for the comparison.

- Compose: no max-only flexible frame analog exactly. `Modifier.widthIn(max=620.dp)` clamps constraints, child can choose less. In a Column with `horizontalAlignment = CenterHorizontally`, a child with `widthIn(max=620)` and content smaller will be content width and centered; if content larger, max. To fill up to max, you'd use `fillMaxWidth(0.?)` or `BoxWithConstraints` + `widthIn`. `fillMaxWidth(fraction)` sets min=max=maxWidth*fraction, so full fill. `widthIn` max only is a cap/hug, closer to Pathland's desired behavior. Compose's `Modifier.widthIn(max=620)` is a constraint clamp, not fill. It centers via parent alignment if smaller. This matches the user's desired Pathland semantics (bounded cap) more than SwiftUI.
- Flutter: `ConstrainedBox(BoxConstraints(maxWidth:620))` combines with parent constraints; child chooses size. It does not force fill to 620. Parent `Center`/`Column(crossAxisAlignment.center)` centers if smaller. If the child is greedy (e.g., `ListView`/`Expanded`?) it fills up to max. This matches a cap/hug, not SwiftUI's fill-to-max. Note Flutter's `Container(width: double.infinity)` with constraints would fill; `ConstrainedBox` alone max doesn't force. So Pathland's cap semantics matches Compose/Flutter more than SwiftUI.
- Flutter `Expanded`/`Flexible` in Row/Column sets tight/loose main-axis constraints; `ConstrainedBox` maxWidth caps. For cross axis, `CrossAxisAlignment.stretch` tightens cross constraints; default center. Pathland's default is hug/start? Pathland default alignment start, unlike Flutter default center. But user explicitly centered parent.
- Ideal:
  - SwiftUI idealWidth: replaces unspecified dimension in proposal. It can influence size when parent proposes unspecified, otherwise flexible frame. It's not fixed.
  - Compose: no ideal; `width(IntrinsicSize.Max/Min)` gives intrinsic; `weight(fill=false)` maybe; `BoxWithConstraints`; `widthIn` + custom. `Modifier.width` is preferred width but incoming constraints can override.
  - Flutter: no ideal; `IntrinsicWidth`/`IntrinsicHeight`, `ConstrainedBox` min/max, `SizedBox`, `LayoutBuilder`; `IntrinsicWidth` sizes to max intrinsic width. `Container(width:)` with constraints. `ConstrainedBox(minWidth: ...)` can set min. Ideal as "preferred natural size" could map to `IntrinsicWidth` or `ConstrainedBox` min? There is no direct equivalent.
- ScrollView:
  - SwiftUI ScrollView expands on scroll axis, hugs cross axis (unless content fills? SwiftUI ScrollView cross axis behavior: ScrollView proposes nil in scroll axis, and its cross size is the proposed cross size? Actually a vertical ScrollView takes full available width by default? In SwiftUI, ScrollView by default fills the available space on the cross axis? Let's recall: `ScrollView(.vertical) { Text(...) }` in a VStack: it takes full width? I think ScrollView is greedy in both axes unless framed? Hmm. SwiftUI ScrollView defaults to fill available space in both directions? Actually `.scrollView` size: vertical ScrollView takes all width and height? It may fill both? But spec says scroll axis greedy, cross hugs. Need check. The spec claims SwiftUI ScrollView cross axis hugs. Is that accurate? Let's verify with SwiftUI docs/search. This matters for spec correctness. Search.

We can specify along which axes a scroll view should scroll. The default is vertical. While a vertical scroll view always becomes exactly as tall as proposed, it has infinite vertical space available for its contents. During layout, a vertical scroll passes on its own proposed width, but it proposes nil for the height to its children. In other words, it tells its children to become their ideal height.
In the example below, we can see how the proposed value of the scroll view propagates through the view tree. Note that the green color has an ideal height , which gets used when the stack proposes a nil height. (If you're wondering why the VStack first propagates to the padded text, it's because it's the least flexible child.)

        "Depending on the relationship a view needs to have with its container, we can choose from three `containerRelativeFrame()` overloads. A view can fill the available width or height, occupy a chosen number of equal portions, or calculate a custom length from the container size. In each case, SwiftUI finds the nearest supported container, such as a window, navigation or tab container, or scroll view, and uses the space it provides after accounting for safe-area insets.

## \# Matching a container dimension

The most direct form of container-relative sizing makes a view match its container along one or more axes. Its first parameter accepts an `Axis.Set` , where we pass `.horizontal` to use the available width, `.vertical` to use the available height, or `[.horizontal, .vertical]` to match both dimensions.

For example, we can present a series of cards in a horizontal scroll view, with each card matching the width of its visible content area.

```
struct  DaysView:  View  {
     var  body:  some View  {
         let  pageMargin:  CGFloat  =  20 ScrollView (. horizontal ) {
             HStack (spacing: pageMargin) {
                 ForEach (dayForecasts) { forecast  in DayForecastCard (forecast: forecast)
                        . containerRelativeFrame (. horizontal )
                }
            }
        }
        . contentMargins (. horizontal , pageMargin)
    }
}
```

The `HStack` isn't a supported container for relative sizing, so SwiftUI continues up the view hierarchy and uses the surrounding `ScrollView` . Its horizontal content margins are removed from the available width, allowing every card to fill the visible content area while preserving space at both edges. Because we only pass the horizontal axis to `containerRelativeFrame()` , the card can determine its own height from its content or aspect ratio.

## \# Dividing a container into equal portions

Matching an entire container dimension works well when one view should fill the available space, but some layouts need to keep several items visible at once.

Let's draft final.

## Comparison: finite `maxWidth` semantics

### SwiftUI

```swift
VStack(alignment: .center) {
    HStack { /* content */ }
        .frame(maxWidth: 620)
}
```

SwiftUI’s frame is a **flexible frame**, not just a CSS cap:

- Only `maxWidth` set: if the parent proposes more than the content size, the frame accepts the proposal **clamped to 620**. So it commonly becomes 620 wide, even when the content is smaller.
- Only `minWidth` set: the frame grows between the content size and the proposal.
- Both `minWidth` and `maxWidth`: SwiftUI clamps the **parent proposal** to that range, largely ignoring content size.
- `idealWidth` is used when the proposal for that dimension is unspecified; it is **not** a fixed width.

So SwiftUI `.frame(maxWidth: 620)` ≈ “fill up to 620,” not “hug content but never exceed 620.”

### Jetpack Compose

```kotlin
Column(horizontalAlignment = Alignment.CenterHorizontally) {
    Box(
        modifier = Modifier.widthIn(max = 620.dp)
    ) { /* content */ }
}
```

Compose is constraint-based:

- `widthIn(max = 620.dp)` adds a max constraint; the child chooses its own size within it.
- The child **does not automatically fill** to 620. A small child stays small and is centered by the parent.
- `fillMaxWidth()` sets `minWidth = maxWidth = available`, so it fills.
- `fillMaxWidth(fraction)` fills a fraction of the available max width.
- `weight` distributes main-axis space in `Row`/`Column`.

This is a **cap/hug** model, not SwiftUI’s flexible fill-to-max model.

### Flutter

```dart
Column(
  crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.center,
  children: [
    ConstrainedBox(
      constraints: const BoxConstraints(maxWidth: 620),
      child: content,
    ),
  ],
)
```

Flutter is also constraint-based:

- `ConstrainedBox(maxWidth: 620)` intersects its constraints with the parent’s; it does **not** force the child to 620.
- A small child stays small; `Center`/`Align` or `Column(crossAxisAlignment: center)` centers it.
- To fill up to 620, use a child that expands, e.g. `SizedBox(width: double.infinity)` or tight constraints.
- Flutter’s `Column` defaults to `CrossAxisAlignment.center`; Pathland’s default is start.

### Summary

| Behavior | SwiftUI `maxWidth: 620` | Compose `widthIn(max = 620.dp)` | Flutter `ConstrainedBox(maxWidth: 620)` | Proposed Pathland `MAX_WIDTH=620` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Small content in a wide parent | Expands to 620 | Stays content-sized | Stays content-sized | Stays content-sized (recommended) |
| Large content | Capped at 620 | Capped at 620 | Capped at 620 | Capped at 620 |
| Fill to available | `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` | `fillMaxWidth()` | `SizedBox(width: double.infinity)` | `WIDTH=FILL` |
| Center the capped box | Parent stack alignment | Parent alignment | Parent `Center`/`Align` | Parent `ALIGNMENT` |

**Recommendation:** make Pathland’s finite `MAX_*` match Compose/Flutter: a **cap/hug constraint**, not SwiftUI’s flexible fill-to-max. Pathland already has an explicit `FILL` kind, and the docs page’s first HStack depends on maxWidth acting as a cap. Matching SwiftUI would make both HStacks expand to their max widths and require a different centering strategy.

## Comparison: `idealWidth` / ideal size

| Framework | Equivalent | Semantics |
|---|---|---|
| SwiftUI | `.frame(idealWidth:)` | A preferred size used when the proposal for that dimension is unspecified; not a fixed size. |
| Compose | No direct equivalent | Closest: `width(IntrinsicSize.Max/Min)` for intrinsic measurement, or `widthIn` bounds. |
| Flutter | No direct equivalent | Closest: `IntrinsicWidth` / `IntrinsicHeight`, or `ConstrainedBox(minWidth:)`. |
| Pathland | `IDEAL_WIDTH/HEIGHT` | Currently mapped to CSS `width/height`, which behaves like a fixed size and can overwrite `WIDTH`. |

**Recommendation:** define `IDEAL_*` as advisory. In v1, either ignore it or only use it when the axis has no proposal and no explicit size. Do **not** treat it as Fixed. This removes the current CSS ordering bug where `IDEAL_WIDTH` can overwrite `WIDTH`.

## Comparison: ScrollView cross axis

| Framework | Vertical ScrollView cross-axis width |
|---|---|
| SwiftUI | Hugs its content width unless a child fills the width; it accepts the proposed height on the scroll axis. |
| Compose | Keeps the incoming width constraints; content width unless a child uses `fillMaxWidth`. |
| Flutter | More parent/child dependent: `SingleChildScrollView` can shrink-wrap the cross axis, while `ListView` generally expands it. |
| Pathland spec | Cross axis hugs; scroll axis is greedy. This matches SwiftUI and Compose. |
| Current Pathland renderers | HTML/Java/TS/GTK treat ScrollView as greedy on both axes; Qt is already correct. |

So the existing `spec/LAYOUT.md` ScrollView rule is correct. The spec work is mainly adding the missing **frame bounds** contract, not rewriting ScrollView.

 ### 9.3 Language adaptation rules
 
 **The three operations are normative; their spellings are not.** A conformant
 DSL MUST expose *configure values*, *apply modifiers*, and *supply children*,
 each available at creation or by chaining (any order), mapped to the host
 language's idioms. The canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) spelling is
 `Text("x").padding(16)`; Java spells values `make(...)` (views) / lowercase
 functions (modifiers) and chains `modifiers(...)` / `children(...)`.

 | single-value shortcut | `make(value)` / `padding(value)` (sugar for the lambda) | `Make(value)` | `Type::new(value)` / `Type(sig)` | `Type(val)` | `Type(val=…)` / `Type(sig)` |
 | apply modifiers | `.modifiers(…)` | `.Modifiers(…)` | `.modifiers(…)` (single or tuple) | `.Modifiers(…)` | `.modifiers(…)` |
 | supply children | `.children(…)` | `.Children(…)` | `.children(vec![…])` / `vstack![…]` | ctor args / `.Children(…)` | `.children(*v)` |
 | creation + chaining | static on the view; chain on the returned builder | static on the view; chain via **extension methods** | associated fn `Type::new`; chain via a **trait** + macros | package ctor; chain via methods | kwargs + methods |
 | same-name static + chain | **builder split** (static on class, chain on builder) | extension methods (separate static class) | assoc fn + trait method | package func + method (not type-scoped) | **not expressible** (methods are last-wins) |
 | `with` name legal | yes | yes (`With`; lowercase `with` is the record keyword) | yes | yes | **no** — `with` is a keyword → kwargs / `configure` |
 | varargs children | yes | `params` | no — slices/arrays or macros | `...` | `*args` |
 | value *is* the modifier | enum OK | **enum can't implement an interface** → `record struct` / static readonly value | enum OK | typed const + method OK | enum member with `apply` OK |

   supply the equivalent single-value modifier form (a `record struct`, a static
   readonly value, or an implicit conversion).

/// always stays valid HTML.
#[must_use]
pub fn node_comment(id: u32, node: &Node) -> String {
    let mut content = format!(" #{} {}", id, component_name(node.component));

        if !text.is_empty() {

            .properties
            .keys()
            .map(|prop| format!("{}={}", property_name(*prop), format_value(node, *prop)))
            .collect();
        let _ = write!(content, ": {}", props.join(", "));
    }
    format!("<!--{} -->", scrub(&content))
}

/// Format a property value for a comment, decoded by its protocol value type.
/// A `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference renders as its token path; everything else is
/// decoded from the stored bits.
fn format_value(node: &Node, prop: u16) -> String {
    if let Some(path) = node.token_refs.get(&prop) {
        return path.clone();
    }
    let Some(bits) = node.properties.get(&prop).copied() else {
        return "?".to_string();
    };
    match value_type_for(prop) {
        value_type::STRING => node
            .strings
            .get(&prop)
            .map(|s| format!("{s:?}"))
            .unwrap_or_else(|| "?".to_string()),
        value_type::COLOR => format!("#{bits:08X}"),
        value_type::U8 => {
            if is_bool_prop(prop) {
                (bits != 0).to_string()
            } else {
                bits.to_string()
            }
        }
        value_type::U32 => {
            if is_mask_prop(prop) {
                format!("0x{bits:08X}")
            } else {
                bits.to_string()
            }
        }
        _ => format_f32(f32::from_bits(bits), prop),
    }
}

/// Format an `F32` property value: `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` sentinels decode to
/// `FILL`/`HUG`; well-known enum codes decode to their names; otherwise a
/// trimmed number.
fn format_f32(v: f32, prop: u16) -> String {
    if prop == property_id::WIDTH || prop == property_id::HEIGHT {
        if v == size::FILL {
            return "FILL".to_string();
        }
        if v == size::HUG_CONTENT {
            return "HUG".to_string();
        }
    }
    if let Some(name) = enum_name(prop, v) {
        return name.to_string();
    }
    format!("{v}")
}

/// Decode a well-known enum property (its numeric code as an `F32`) to a
/// friendly name; `None` when the property isn't a known enum or the code is
/// unknown (the caller then shows the raw number).
fn enum_name(prop: u16, v: f32) -> Option<&'static str> {
    let code = v.round() as i32;
    match prop {
        property_id::ALIGNMENT => match code {
            0 => Some("Leading"),
            1 => Some("Center"),
            2 => Some("Trailing"),
            3 => Some("Fill"),
            _ => None,
        },
        property_id::TEXT_ALIGNMENT => match code {
            0 => Some("Leading"),
            1 => Some("Center"),
            2 => Some("Trailing"),
            _ => None,
        },
        property_id::TRUNCATION_MODE => match code {
            0 => Some("Head"),
            1 => Some("Middle"),
            2 => Some("Tail"),
            _ => None,
        },
        property_id::SHAPE_KIND => match code {
            0 => Some("Circle"),
            1 => Some("Rectangle"),
            2 => Some("RoundedRectangle"),
            3 => Some("Capsule"),
            4 => Some("Ellipse"),
            5 => Some("Path"),
            _ => None,
        },
        property_id::CONTENT_MODE => match code {
            0 => Some("Fit"),
            1 => Some("Fill"),
            _ => None,
        },
        property_id::TRANSITION => match code {
            0 => Some("None"),
            1 => Some("PlatformDefault"),
            2 => Some("Fade"),
            3 => Some("Slide"),
            4 => Some("Scale"),
            _ => None,
        },
        property_id::NAV_CHROME => match code {
            0 => Some("PlatformDefault"),
            1 => Some("Custom"),
            _ => None,
        },
        property_id::TOGGLE_STYLE => match code {
            0 => Some("Switch"),
            1 => Some("Checkbox"),
            2 => Some("Button"),
            _ => None,
        },
        property_id::CONTROL_SIZE => match code {
            0 => Some("Small"),
            1 => Some("Regular"),
            2 => Some("Large"),
            _ => None,
        },
        property_id::DATE_PICKER_MODE => match code {
            0 => Some("Date"),
            1 => Some("Time"),
            2 => Some("DateAndTime"),
            _ => None,
        },
        property_id::PICKER_STYLE => match code {
            0 => Some("Menu"),
            1 => Some("Segmented"),
            2 => Some("Wheel"),
            3 => Some("RadioGroup"),
            _ => None,
        },
        property_id::FONT_STYLE => match code {
            0 => Some("Normal"),
            1 => Some("Italic"),
            _ => None,
        },
        property_id::FONT_DESIGN => match code {
            0 => Some("Default"),
            1 => Some("Serif"),
            2 => Some("Rounded"),
            3 => Some("Monospaced"),
            _ => None,
        },
        property_id::TEXT_CASE => match code {
            0 => Some("None"),
            1 => Some("Uppercase"),
            2 => Some("Lowercase"),
            _ => None,
        },
        _ => None,
    }
}

fn is_bool_prop(prop: u16) -> bool {
    matches!(
        prop,
        property_id::SELECTED
            | property_id::IS_SECURE
            | property_id::IS_INDETERMINATE
            | property_id::VISIBLE
            | property_id::ENABLED
            | property_id::CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS
            | property_id::UNDERLINE
            | property_id::STRIKETHROUGH
            | property_id::COLOR_INVERT
            | property_id::ALLOWS_HIT_TESTING
            | property_id::FIXED_SIZE_HORIZONTAL
            | property_id::FIXED_SIZE_VERTICAL
    )
}

fn is_mask_prop(prop: u16) -> bool {
    prop == property_id::EVENT_LISTENERS || prop == property_id::BORDER_EDGES
}

/// Ensure a comment never contains `--` (which would terminate it) and never
/// ends with `-` (which would make the closing `-->` ambiguous).
fn scrub(s: &str) -> String {
    let mut out = s.replace("--", "- -");
    if out.ends_with('-') {
        out.push(' ');
    }
    out
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    fn node(component: u16, props: &[(u16, u32)], strings: &[(u16, &str)]) -> Node {
        Node {
            component,
            text: None,
            properties: props.iter().copied().collect(),
            strings: strings
                .iter()
                .map(|(k, v)| (*k, v.to_string()))
                .collect(),

    }

        assert_eq!(component_name(component_type::TEXT), "Text");
        assert_eq!(component_name(component_type::TEXT_FIELD), "TextField");

    }

 This document provides essential context for AI agents (or human contributors) working on the **Pathland** protocol. It captures the project's direction, architectural decisions, and implementation details to ensure consistency.
